title: Subordinate clauses and case patterns
matching: Typed answers ignore letter case, extra spaces, apostrophe style and final . ! or ? punctuation. Accents and every other character count. Multiple-choice answers must match exactly.

lessons.title: Weil clauses with the verb at the end
lessons.explanation: A weil clause gives a reason and is a subordinate clause: the finite verb moves to the end. Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin. A comma separates the clauses. If the weil clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: Weil ich müde bin, bleibe ich zu Hause. With a modal verb the finite modal is last: weil er arbeiten muss. A separable verb is written together again: weil er früh aufsteht.

lessons.title: Dass clauses after reporting and opinion verbs
lessons.explanation: Use a dass clause to report what someone thinks, knows or says. After verbs such as glauben, denken, wissen, sagen and hoffen, a comma and dass introduce a subordinate clause with the finite verb at the end: Ich glaube, dass er kommt. Do not confuse dass (conjunction) with das (article or pronoun). A dass clause can also start the sentence, but at this level use it after the main clause.

lessons.title: Embedded questions with question words
lessons.explanation: A question can sit inside another sentence. The question word opens the clause and the finite verb moves to the end: Ich weiß nicht, wo er wohnt. Common openers are Ich weiß nicht, Kannst du mir sagen and Sie fragt. Use wo, wann, wie, warum, wer and was as in direct questions, but do not invert the verb and subject. A separable verb is written together again: wann der Kurs anfängt.

lessons.title: Accusative and dative in frequent verb and preposition patterns
lessons.explanation: Some prepositions always take the accusative: für, ohne, durch, gegen, um. Others always take the dative: mit, nach, bei, von, zu, aus, seit. Many verbs also take a dative object: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken. With verbs like schenken or geben, the person receiving is dative and the thing is accusative: Ich schenke meiner Mutter ein Buch. Learn the case with the preposition or verb.
